item.content:encoded:
Not only do I have no problem accepting this as a realistic installation, I am mildly surprised that it wasn't based on an IRL thing.

Not all artists are sociopathic ass-hats, and not all art consumers are imbecilic failures of Darwinism; but the community has no shortage of both.
This is of course, merely my own opinion. But in partial support of the hypothesis, I submit this. An art installation with known, if not intentional, neurological impact; with a mandatory waiver explaining the risks with particular emphasis on the risk of seizure; and at least 3 seizure-prone individuals went in anyway.
Congratulations! Took a few days longer then I expected, but I suppose it's not for everybody.

I went and reread the comments, as the son of an artist who dabbled in a bit of any and everything, seeing a large sum of the artworld, I must say a few things

item.content:encoded:
Initial reaction: FUCKING… *gesticulates wildly at the screen* THIS!!!

Full thought: See, here's the thing; nothing in the article stated anywhere that all of those people were stupid in quick succession. Nor that the entirety of the human race is objectively that stupid. There *are*, however, people objectively stupid enough to go "Oh yeah, right, that's not an ACTUAL legally binding waver, and those spinning 'blades' just have red paint on them. I'll bet they're not even sharp, or they're those instant-brake things that can't actually cut anyone, here watch I'll-" and then the exhibit is shut down for five minutes while they drag the guy out holding the bloody stump and screaming. Then, a couple of days later, some other person - through stupidity or willful obstinance - goes "Oh ha ha, needles full of diseases, yeah look at me I'm- Ow?" And then another time, someoe pulls the lever on their own electric chair.

And yes, a sealed-tight shower-sized chamber (with nothing saying the door doesn't lock when you push the button) spraying pressurized liquid nitrogen on you would suck horribly for a very short amount of time and then you're dead from various effects.

item.content:encoded:
I'm pretty much in agreement here. I don't see it as stupid so much as curious. Like watching a cat playing with something that you just know is going to turn on him, but the cat does it anyway due to curiosity and instinct. That's the thing, curiosity in humans is instinctive.

It reminds me, in a way, of one of my SCPs, the Ear Candles. Sure, the candles themselves are anomalous, but the fact that people will stick one in their ear and light it is not. People will do things like that, poke at the stick or touch the spinning blade, due to the incomplete thinking that humans do in part, and our curious nature.

One quibble, though: Virulent injections aren't an instant kill, they take time to incubate before the effects take hold. And the trouble with putting a vial of Marburg Virus or Smallpox is that it will not only take several days or weeks for the person to die, but he's likely to kick off an epidemic in his city or country because of it. There's a reason why Smallpox has been eradicated in the wild, it's one of the big killers of mankind and one of the early vaccines. But it's contagious as all hell.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
+ response
- Hide text

It's not intended as sneering contempt, and I'm definitely not criticising the art community.

Then I'm not sure what you're trying to convey here, because what you have is an artist making an exhibit that's an "homage to stupidity", which is then patronized by hordes of stupid people, while the gallery owner remarks on how people are too stupid to get it.

I actually spent a decent amount of yesterday coming up with these ideas for installations to pitch myself, then realised that there was no way anybody would actually let genuinely dangerous stuff into an art gallery, no matter how strongly worded the waiver is.

You are correct, no one would ever do that, which is why this article makes no sense. I've seen other people suggest that the artwork is actually anomalous, which would mean another entry in the Thing What Compels You ranks. I don't think that's what you're going for. Either way, I'm not buying it.

It's not a case of "look how stupid everyone in the world is", that's simply the perspective of the (fictional) artist.

Except you're lending credence to the artist's viewpoint by having people show up and act exactly as stupid as he imagines them to be.

If an exhibit like this were actually put anywhere, some people would be sufficiently curious about whether there was any actual danger, or simply the illusion of danger; it's curiosity, not stupidity.

No one with anything close to a right mind is going look at a spinning circular saw and go "maaaybe it's an illlluuuusion" and stick their hand into it. That's not curiosity, that's complete suicidal disregard for one's safety.

Also, even if the art isn't anomalous, it is still deadly, and deadly art is (I think, and feel free to disagree) within the bounds of AWCY's established purview.

I loathe AWCY, but even so I don't think their point is merely art what kills you. Unlike the rest of my commentary, I'm pretty sure a majority of users would agree, based on the material put out on the site. I have never viewed "killing people" as being their chief aim, if they even have one.

And it wasn't really "forced" from my end, so I'm kind of confused why people are seeing it like that.

Let me be clear here; it's ME saying that it's forced. I don't see anyone else making that statement. And yes, I think a story that would have had nothing at all do with the Foundation save for a tacked-on AWCY reference is forced.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: As said in the story, the cubicle is airtight, so at the very least asphyxiation is imminent. Also, the difference between a short burst of liquid nitrogen and a continuous, pressurised stream is important. The short burst will form a bubble of the nitrogen gas between your skin and the rest of it (which, as you said, is commonly known as the 'Science Effect'), but if you've got a pressurised spray of the stuff, that bubble isn't going to support anything, and your skin's going to freeze very quickly. Admittedly, he's not going to die instantly, but the shock (especially considering it's hitting his head and face, so it would also probably burst his eyes as the ice expands) would knock him out within a few seconds.

I will say this: the narrative is kind of telly. I mean, you just tell us what his aim is, which is absolutely unnecessary since it all comes out by the end.

So while this could use some polishing, it's still kind of great. It probably does have to do with the lower of expectations created by the title (which, by the way, would not be nearly as great without the 'wowee'), but it's nevertheless fun and worth some thought. I mean honestly, the anomaly here is the people, if anything. You sit back and think, "What person in their right mind (assuming the waivers are clear enough) would stick their hand into a moving saw? The answer is "maybe you". Because while we all like to think of ourselves as sane and rational individuals, the fact is everyone is perfectly capable of abandoning reason at the drop of a hat and doing something stupid. Pretty awesome.
